title: Produce crop in a hydroponic system

lessons.title: Hydroponic systems and their components
lessons.html:
What is hydroponics?

Hydroponics is growing plants without soil, supplying all nutrients in a water-based nutrient solution. Roots grow either directly in the solution or in an inert growing medium. In South Africa, hydroponics is widely used under tunnels and greenhouses for tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, lettuce, herbs and strawberries. It allows high yields per square metre, efficient water use and production on poor or limited land, but demands precise management.

Common system types

SystemHow it worksTypical crops
Open bag or slab (drain-to-waste) systemsPlants grow in bags of coir, sawdust, perlite or similar; nutrient solution is dripped on and excess drains awayTomatoes, cucumbers, peppers
Nutrient film technique (NFT)A thin film of solution flows continuously along sloped gullies over the rootsLettuce, herbs, leafy greens
Deep water culture (floating raft)Plants float on rafts with roots in aerated solutionLettuce, leafy greens
Ebb and flowTrays are flooded periodically and drainedSeedlings, potted plants
Recirculating media systemsDrain water is collected, disinfected and reusedVarious

Key components

  • Structure: tunnel or greenhouse with suitable covering, ventilation and shade netting.
  • Water source: water quality tested for EC, pH, sodium, chloride, bicarbonates and microbes; poor water may need treatment.
  • Nutrient tanks and dosing: stock solutions (usually separate A and B tanks so calcium and sulphates or phosphates do not precipitate), injectors or dosing computers.
  • Irrigation system: pump, filters, drippers or gullies, timers or controllers.
  • Growing medium: coir, perlite, sawdust, rockwool or none (NFT, rafts).
  • Monitoring instruments: EC and pH meters, thermometers, drain collection containers, light and humidity sensors.

Advantages and risks

Advantages include high yields, controlled nutrition and less soil-borne disease. Risks include rapid crop failure if pumps, power or dosing fail, high setup costs and fast spread of root diseases in recirculating systems. Backup power or alarms are important.

lessons.title: Managing nutrition, climate and crop health
lessons.html:
Nutrient solution management

  • Recipes: use crop- and stage-specific recipes from a reputable supplier or adviser. Mix stock solutions accurately and never mix concentrated A and B stock directly.
  • EC: measures total nutrient concentration. Check the dripper (input) EC and the drain EC daily. A rising drain EC indicates salt build-up and the need to adjust or increase drainage, within the adviser's guidelines.
  • pH: affects nutrient availability; maintain within the target range for the crop and system, usually by adjusting with acid as instructed.
  • Drain percentage: in drain-to-waste systems, measure the volume drained versus volume applied to judge whether irrigation is correct for the weather and crop stage.
  • Calibrate meters with standard solutions regularly and record readings.

Climate management

  • Ventilate to control temperature and humidity; high humidity favours fungal diseases, very high temperatures reduce fruit set.
  • Use shade netting or whitewash in hot periods; adjust irrigation frequency to radiation and temperature.
  • Ensure air movement around plants.

Crop management

  • Plant healthy seedlings from a reputable nursery.
  • Train vine crops on strings, remove side shoots and lower leaves as specified.
  • Support pollination: in tunnels, tomatoes are often pollinated by vibrating the flower trusses regularly or by other approved methods.
  • Harvest regularly at the correct maturity.

Pest and disease control

  • Hygiene: footbaths, clean tools, remove plant waste, disinfect between crops.
  • Insect screens and double doors to exclude whitefly, thrips and aphids.
  • Scout weekly with yellow and blue sticky traps.
  • Use IPM: biological control agents where available, registered products only per label, observing pre-harvest intervals.
  • Watch for root diseases such as Pythium in recirculating systems; disinfect recirculated water.

Safety

Wear gloves and eye protection when handling acids and concentrated nutrients; add acid to water, never water to acid. Keep electrical equipment away from water and protected by earth leakage devices.

Records

Record EC, pH, drain percentage, irrigation volumes, climate data, pest counts, sprays, yields and costs daily or weekly.

Key points

  • Hydroponics supplies all nutrients in solution, with or without inert media.
  • Keep A and B stocks separate and follow crop-specific recipes.
  • Monitor input and drain EC, pH and drain percentage daily.
  • Manage ventilation, humidity and shading to suit the crop.
  • Use strict hygiene, screens, scouting and IPM; keep detailed records.
